This analysis reveals that test repeatability is fundamentally about managing uncertainty in our knowledge systems. Non-repeatable tests introduce epistemic doubt - when a test fails, we cannot immediately know whether we've found a bug or encountered randomness. This uncertainty tax compounds through the development process, making each debugging session an exercise in distinguishing signal from noise. The mathematical formalization shows that even small amounts of non-determinism (ρ < 0.9) can double or triple debugging time, validating the intuition that flaky tests are among the most expensive technical debts. The principle ultimately argues for treating repeatability as a first-class design constraint, not an afterthought.
